summary: Deep technical profiling session focused on kernel selection trade-offs, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM behavior, CUDA graphs benefits, and quantization impacts on throughput and latency. Discussed KV cache implications for long-context workloads and on-prem/VPC constraints for running private inference. Agreed next steps: share benchmarks, run customer-specific workloads, and plan an on-prem pilot.
transcript:
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Samir Patel from Redwood. Lauren and I will run through the profiling results and then dig into any infra questions.
[00:28] Mike: Hi Samir, Priya, Jorge here. We really want to understand where the perf wins are between TensorRT-LLM and vLLM, especially for our long-context customer scoring pipeline.
[01:02] Lauren: Cool, quick agenda: kernel selection, cudagraphs, quantization effects, KV cache behavior, and then infra/VPC notes. This is pretty hands-on so interrupt anytime.
[01:40] Priya: Quick context — our current infra is a mix of GCP A100s and some on-prem H100s. We see guest latency of ~180ms for 1k token seq on our baseline FP16 setup, and throughput is jittery under burst.
[02:05] Lauren: Got it. We ran a 1k prompt sweep on A100 80GB, comparing vLLM (master branch + some local patches) vs TensorRT-LLM (TRT-LLM) with cudagraphs enabled. Important note: transcription has some small typos, TENserRT-LLM in my notes, haha.
[02:40] Samir: Early top-line: TRT-LLM + cudagraphs tends to reduce per-token latency by ~15-35% at steady state for autoregressive workloads, but warmup and kernel selection complexity can add overhead if sequence lengths vary a lot.
[03:10] Mike: Can you give concrete numbers? Our SLO is 100ms p95 for 512 tokens.
[03:30] Lauren: Sure — for 512 tokens, FP16 baseline: vLLM ~95-110ms p95 depending on batch, TRT-LLM + cudagraphs median around 75-90ms p95 in our runs. But note: when enabling INT8 / 4-bit quant (q4/awq), latency can drop further, but quality regressions depend on model and calibration.
[04:05] Priya: We care about both latency and output fidelity — we can't accept hallucination regressions. Did you run evals?
[04:20] Lauren: Yes, we ran a quick BLEU/likelihood style diff and a few task-specific prompts. On many LLMs, AWQ/INT8 had negligible delta for scoring tasks, but for creative generation there were edge cases. We'll share the eval artifacts. Link: https://redwood.internal/benchmarks/ql-trt-vllm-11-03 (note: internal link).
[05:00] Jorge: From infra side, cudagraphs sounds great but how does it interact with dynamic batching and KV cache? We do a lot of streaming multitenant requests.
[05:25] Lauren: Good question. CUDA graphs capture a static sequence of CUDA work; they work best when the kernel launch patterns are stable — e.g., fixed seq len or when you partition by sequence-length buckets. For dynamic streaming with KV cache you can still use cudagraphs for the fixed parts (attention kernels) but you need to manage graph repr visits — some runtimes do graph re-instantiation or use a small set of graphs per seq-length bucket.
[06:10] Samir: Kernel selection matter: TRT-LLM runtime does aggressive kernel fusion and will pick tensor cores vs fp16 matmuls differently than vLLM which relies more on kernel library mixes. That leads to the observed latency gaps, but also to situations where TRT requires careful tuning for short sequences to avoid overhead.
[06:45] Priya: Any comments on KV cache memory usage — our long context runs up to 65k tokens per session.
[07:05] Lauren: KV cache scales linearly with context and number of layers; with 65k tokens you'll be memory bound on a single GPU for large models. Two patterns we recommend: 1) prefix sharding across GPUs (split layers/KV across devices) or 2) truncation + on-demand remote KV (somewhat experimental). Also quantized KV storage (4-bit storage) is viable for many models to reduce footprint.
[07:50] Mike: When you say prefix sharding, is that supported in TRT-LLM?
[08:10] Samir: TRT-LLM has tensor parallel and pipeline options; prefix sharding needs orchestration. Redwood's runtime can do smart routing so you don't have to manage it manually — we can route long-context sessions to dedicated nodes or use a multi-GPU allocation.
[08:40] Lauren: Quick microbenchmark: for a 2048 token workload, batch size 1, vLLM w/ FP16 was ~210 tokens/s, TRT-LLM w/ cudagraphs was ~270 tokens/s on A100. With INT8 quant on TRT-LLM we saw up to ~340 tokens/s but with a 0.5-1.5% drop on a small quality metric for one model.
[09:20] Priya: Interesting. What about kernel selection variability across GPUs — does H100 change the picture?
[09:40] Lauren: H100 improves tensor core throughput and has new matmul shapes; TRT-LLM gains more on H100 in our tests — relative uplift vs vLLM was larger (20-40% improvement) because TRT fused kernels better exploit DPX and Hopper features. But these numbers depend on model architecture and sequence length distribution.
[10:10] Mike: Can cudagraphs cause latency spikes during graph instantiation? We saw a cold-start spike.
[10:30] Lauren: Yes — first few invocations may incur graph capture/compile overhead. Strategies: pre-warm graphs with representative inputs, or maintain a warm pool. Redwood's dedicated offering can prepopulate graphs on nodes as part of deployment.
[11:05] Jorge: On the VPC/on-prem side — if we want to run private, what are the storage and logging constraints? We have strict data residency and can't ship logs off-prem.
[11:30] Samir: Redwood Private supports a customer-managed control plane and you can configure audit logs to stay in your VPC. We'll provide KMS integration and HSM options. For on-prem, you typically need an NFS/CEPH or local SSD staging area for model artifacts and logs; we can advise on sizing based on model + KV cache footprint.
[12:00] Priya: Can you re-run the kernel selection example? I want to understand where TRT picks fused kernels vs pointwise.
[12:20] Lauren: Yeah, in our profiler trace you'll see multiple kernel variants named something like "gelu_fused_v2" vs "gelu_pointwise"; TRT prefers fused when profitable but fusion increases register pressure and can be slower for short sequences. There's also changing heuristics per layer; one layer might prefer a different layout.
[13:05] Samir: We also instrumented CUDA Graph replay vs direct launch. For steady state, cudagraphs removes launch overhead and PCIe sync cost which matters for small kernels executed repeatedly. But if your workload has many unique shapes, graph churn can become a net-negative.
[13:45] Priya: Any tips on batching? We need low p95 but high throughput overall.
[14:00] Lauren: For mixed latency/throughput targets, we recommend a two-tier pool: low-latency nodes with small batch sizes and no/limited batching, and throughput nodes with aggressive batching and caching. Redwood can route by policy: latency-first requests to low-latency pool, background/cheap requests to throughput pool.
[14:35] Mike: How does KV cache affect batching?
[14:50] Lauren: KV cache reduces repeated compute for prefixes, but when caching is used, you often see higher effective throughput for repeated prefixes. However, cached keys are per-session and complicate multi-tenant batching: you may need to batch across different offests, so a smart batch aligner is required.
[15:25] Jorge: Any memory/cost numbers for KV cache for 65k context?
[15:40] Lauren: Very rough: for a 70B model with 64 layers, per-token KV storage might be ~2-3KB token (depends on dtype and layer), so 65k tokens -> ~130-195MB per session? Wait that's off, let me correct: actually per-token KV can be ~1-2*layer*head_dim floats — it's model-specific. We will provide precise numbers from our profiler per model.
[16:10] Priya: Let's discuss quantization. Which schemes did you test?
[16:25] Lauren: We tested FP16 baseline, TRT INT8 calibrations, AWQ 4-bit, and NF4-style 4-bit. AWQ gave best accuracy/size tradeoff in our tests for the scoring tasks. With AWQ we saw approx 2.5-3x memory reduction vs FP16 and latency improvements in the 20-50% range depending on kernels.
[17:00] Mike: Are those quantized runs compatible with cudagraphs?
[17:15] Lauren: Yes, generally. However, quantized kernels occasionally require different kernel variants which affects graph reuse. That means you should generate graphs per quantization profile. In multi-profile fleets, pre-generate graphs for each profile.
[17:50] Priya: Did you see any model types that don't quantize well?
[18:10] Lauren: Very large sparse-adapted models and some RLHF-tuned models had larger deltas — not huge but above our thresholds for generation tasks. For scoring/classification tasks they were mostly fine.
[18:40] Samir: We also measured kernel-level utilization via nvprof / Nsight traces; interestingly some attention kernels were memory-bound, others compute-bound. Kernel selection heuristics in TRT-LLM prefer compute-fused versions where compute is the bottleneck.
[19:10] Mike: For the bench you mentioned, how did you measure fairness between runtimes?
[19:25] Lauren: We aligned runtime configs: same model weights, same prompt set, same seq-len distribution, and we used steady-state measurements after warm-up. We also used identical power caps and pinned CPU affinities. There's still noise but we ran >1k samples per config.
[19:58] Priya: Any artifact links?
[20:10] Samir: Yep — bench deck + raw logs + eval diffs: https://redwood.internal/benchmarks/ql-trt-vllm-11-03 (internal). We'll send a share link.
[20:35] Jorge: On the orchestration side, if we want auto-fallback (e.g., if TRT node is saturated), can Redwood route to vLLM nodes with graceful degradation?
[20:50] Samir: Yes, smart routing is core to the Redwood runtime — policy-based routing by latency, cost, and region. You can set fallbacks to multi-choice model variants. Note that model outputs may differ slightly between variants, so we recommend A/B evals.
[21:20] Lauren: One more micro-optimization: layer-norm fusing reduced a lot of small kernels which helped p95 for short sequences. TRT-LLM tends to do more layer fusion out of the box.
[21:50] Mike: For on-prem H100s, anything special?
[22:05] Lauren: For H100s, ensure your CUDA and cuDNN versions align with TRT-LLM supported stack. Also watch for MIG-like partitioning — H100 has more capability but also requires tuning for DPX/matrix multiply shapes.
[22:35] Priya: Are you using cudNN or custom kernels in TRT-LLM?
[22:50] Lauren: A mix. TRT-LLM uses TensorRT-fused kernels and custom CUDA kernels where needed. vLLM uses standard kernels and community-optimized kernels; that difference explains a lot of perf variance.
[23:20] Samir: We also tried graph-level caching where we maintain a catalog of graphs keyed by (seq_len, batch, quant_profile). That reduced churn but increases catalog size. Tradeoffs matter.
[23:50] Jorge: For catalog size, any rough storage numbers?
[24:05] Lauren: A single graph binary can be tens to hundreds of KB, multiply by a few hundred graph variants for many seq/batch combos -> tens to low hundreds of MB, so it's reasonable to store locally on node SSDs.
[24:45] Priya: How to measure real-world p95 under production patterns?
[25:00] Samir: We advise replaying production traces through the runtime. Redwood has a trace replay tool that can simulate multi-tenant arrival patterns, KV cache hits, etc. We also instrument token-level latency metrics in the console.
[25:35] Priya: Did you test 4-bit quant with retraining or just post-training quant?
[25:50] Lauren: Mostly post-training quantization (PTQ) and AWQ. QAT (quant-aware fine-tuning) usually gives better fidelity but is heavier. For scoring tasks PTQ+AWQ was often enough.
[26:20] Mike: What about mixed precision fallbacks? Eg keep some layers in fp16, others in int8.
[26:35] Lauren: Yes, hybrid quantization — keep sensitive layers in fp16 and quantize others — gives good balance. TRT-LLM supports mixed profiles; vLLM requires more custom config.
[27:00] Priya: Let's talk about reproducibility — we need deterministic outputs across nodes for audit.
[27:15] Samir: Determinism is tricky: quantization, fused kernels, and non-deterministic cuBLAS algorithms can cause tiny diffs. You can force deterministic algorithms, but sometimes at perf cost. We can help quantify the tradeoff.
[27:50] Jorge: For our compliance, we need audit logs and per-request token level traces. Is that feasible?
[28:05] Samir: Yes, Redwood Console supports token-level traces and per-request audit logs. For private/on-prem deployments the logs can be stored in your S3 or local object store.
[28:35] Priya: Any pitfalls we should avoid during pilot?
[28:50] Lauren: Common pitfalls: 1) under-provisioning KV memory for long contexts; 2) not warming cudagraphs before load tests; 3) failing to bucket seq lengths for graph reuse; 4) ignoring mixed-precision per-layer sensitivity.
[29:20] Mike: Can you walk through an example graph trace?
[29:35] Lauren: Sure — in the profiler trace you'll see repeated captures of attention and matmul kernels. When shapes are stable, the graph replays with minimal CPU overhead. When shapes change, you see new graph captures, which is where spikes comes.
[30:10] Priya: In your logs, what was the graph churn rate?
[30:25] Lauren: For a mixed seq workload without bucketing, churn was ~20% of requests causing a new graph capture. With bucketing into 4 buckets, churn dropped to <2%.
[30:55] Samir: On the handoff to ops: if you run Redwood Dedicated, we can predefine buckets based on your histograms and pre-generate graphs per node.
[31:20] Jorge: What about NUMA / CPU affinity for capture?
[31:35] Lauren: Capture is CPU-heavy; pin capture threads and isolate cores for cudagraph captures to reduce jitter. Also keep SSD local for graph binaries.
[32:00] Priya: Do you have a recommended default batching policy?
[32:15] Lauren: Start with conservative batch sizes for p95 targets: batch 1-4 for low-latency; batch 8-16 for throughput nodes. Use dynamic max-batch with latency-aware thresholds.
[32:45] Mike: Do you have real customer examples?
[32:55] Samir: Yes — one fintech customer moved short-latency scoring to TRT-LLM with cudagraphs and quantization and reduced cost per request by ~35% while improving p95. We'll anonymize and include a case study.
[33:25] Priya: About accuracy thresholds — who defines acceptable delta? We need measurable gates.
[33:40] Lauren: We recommend task-specific evals: perplexity shifts, embedding cosine thresholds, and task metrics. Redwood's eval pipeline can auto-run and alert on regressions.
[34:05] Jorge: If we run on-prem, how do upgrades work? We want control over TRT versions.
[34:20] Samir: In Private you control the runtime version; Redwood provides upgrade packages and can do managed upgrades if you want. We keep an upgrade matrix for CUDA/TensorRT/CUDNN.
[34:50] Priya: For endpoints, do you recommend mixed fleet (some nodes TRT, some vLLM)?
[35:05] Lauren: Yes, mixed fleets give flexibility: TRT for high-throughput steady-state, vLLM for experimental or fallbacks. Make sure to run A/B evals and have output normalization if you need consistent downstream checks.
[35:35] Mike: Any monitoring recommendations?
[35:50] Samir: Monitor per-token latency, kernel occupancy, GPU memory headroom, graph churn, and KV hit rates. Also track end-to-end p95 and throughput per model. Redwood Console exposes those metrics.
[36:20] Priya: Does graph reuse work across models?
[36:35] Lauren: No, graphs are model-specific because they embed layer shapes and weights in the capture. You need per-model graph catalogs.
[36:55] Jorge: For multi-tenant, do you isolate graphs per-tenant?
[37:10] Samir: You can namespace graphs per-tenant or maintain a shared catalog and tag entries. Namespacing simplifies compliance at the cost of catalog duplication.
[37:40] Priya: Let's talk about the next technical steps for us — we want a benchmark with our prompt set and both A100/H100.
[37:55] Lauren: We'll run a 1k-prompt sweep on your sample set, on A100 and H100, configs: vLLM FP16, TRT-LLM FP16+cudagraphs, TRT-LLM INT8, AWQ 4-bit. We'll return median/p95 tokens/s and per-prompt quality diffs.
[38:25] Mike: For H100 we can provide operator access to test nodes.
[38:40] Jorge: We'll open a service account and a temporary VPC peering for bench data.
[38:55] Samir: Great. We'll also include guidance on file system sizing for graph catalogs and KV cache planning.
[39:20] Priya: Is there any recommended model quantization pipeline?
[39:35] Lauren: AWQ tooling -> calibration dataset -> small PTQ run -> eval; if unacceptable, try hybrid quant or QAT. For TRT-specific INT8, you need calibration caches. We'll share tooling.
[40:00] Mike: Any security concerns with caching keys?
[40:15] Samir: KV cache contains intermediate activations; treat it as sensitive. Encrypt at rest and in memory if possible; Redwood Private supports KMS and mlock-like protection for caches.
[40:40] Jorge: For on-prem, can we use HSM for keys?
[40:55] Samir: Yes, HSM/KMS integration supported. We'll share the integration docs.
[41:20] Priya: Let's circle back to model differences — did you profile an MPT-style vs LLaMA-style architecture?
[41:35] Lauren: We profiled LLaMA-derivatives, MPT, and a proprietary 70B. Some architecture specifics changed kernel mix — wider heads vs deeper layers change memory vs compute balance, which shifts which kernels are optimal.
[42:05] Mike: Did you observe any non-linear scaling with batch?
[42:20] Lauren: Yes — small batches see linear-ish, but once kernels saturate tensor cores you get diminishing returns. For some configs batch 4->8 gave big win, 8->16 smaller. Also NVLink/NIC throughput matters if you do model/prefix sharding.
[42:50] Priya: Will Redwood help tune kernel heuristics?
[43:05] Samir: Yes, our SE team can help tune runtime heuristics and pre-generate graphs per your distributions. That's part of the pilot.
[43:30] Jorge: Any failure modes we should watch for?
[43:45] Lauren: Graph cache corruption, mismatched CUDA/TensorRT versions, and running out of pinned memory for KV cache. We add health checks to detect those.
[44:10] Mike: How do you debug a sudden p95 regression?
[44:25] Samir: Start with graph churn metrics, kernel tail latencies, NVLink saturation, and KV hit-rate drop. Redwood traces token-level lat spikes in the console to help triage.
[44:50] Priya: Can you show a quick trace snippet?
[45:05] Lauren: (shared screen) here's a timeline — you can see repeated captures, then a big spike when a new graph compiles. Also see that attention kernel had a 2.5x tail compared to median.
[45:35] Jorge: For production, do you recommend a warm pool size?
[45:50] Samir: Warm pool depends on your concurrency; a small pool of 5-10 pre-warmed nodes often mitigates cold starts. Dedicated reserved capacity can make this economical.
[46:20] Priya: Any tips on metrics thresholds?
[46:35] Lauren: Track p50/p90/p95 per token and watch for step changes after deploys; set alerts on graph churn rate >5% or KV hit rate drop >10%.
[47:00] Mike: We'll need a secure way to transfer model weights for on-prem.
[47:15] Samir: Use S3-compatible signed URLs into your private bucket or use air-gapped transfer. We'll support both.
[47:40] Jorge: Is the Redwood runtime containerized?
[47:55] Lauren: Yes, containerized with optional privileged device access. For on-prem we provide helm charts and a managed operator if you want.
[48:20] Priya: Quick Q: did you test sequence bucketing impact on GPU utilization?
[48:35] Lauren: Bucketing improved utilization by ~12-18% in our mixed workloads by stabilizing graph reuse and increasing effective batch packing.
[49:00] Samir: Another small note: kernel autotuning can pick suboptimal kernels if the profiler windows are short. Longer profiling windows and repeated runs improve autotuner decisions.
[49:30] Mike: How do you handle model rollouts with different quantization profiles?
[49:45] Samir: Use feature flags and canary routes. Redwood supports per-route rollout percentages with automatic rollback if perf/quality regressions exceed thresholds.
[50:10] Priya: Will you include the API for routing policies in the docs?
[50:25] Samir: Yes, we'll include example configs.
[50:45] Jorge: Any notable differences in power draw between TRT vs vLLM?
[51:00] Lauren: TRT often uses GPU more efficiently for steady loads so power per token drops. For short, bursty workloads the differences shrink.
[51:30] Mike: Let's confirm who does what post-call.
[51:45] Samir: Action items summarized in the meeting notes. Lauren will run per-customer bench, I'll send pricing, and Quantify will share prompts and infra access.
[52:10] Priya: Thanks. One last question — how to measure drift after quantization updates?
[52:25] Lauren: Run periodic evals on gold prompt sets and log metrics in Redwood Console; set regression alerts. We can automate weekly checks.
[52:55] Jorge: On the peering piece — we'll check firewall rules and share required ports.
[53:10] Mike: Ok that sounds good.
[53:20] Samir: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the deck and raw logs.
[53:35] Priya: Appreciate it.
[53:50] (meeting ends)
